why_how.text: Road markings guide, warn and regulate traffic in red, yellow or white, alone or combined.
Yellow center lines mark two-way traffic, and their pattern decides who may pass.

scenario.text: Zoe drives on a road where a solid yellow line is on her side and a broken yellow line is on the other side.

reasoning.text: A broken yellow line beside a solid yellow line allows passing only from the broken side.

result.text: Zoe does not pass; only drivers on the broken side may.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a solid yellow line on your side never lets you cross it.

correction.text: From the solid-yellow side you may cross only for pedestrians, bicyclists or scooter and skateboard riders with the far lane clear.

memory_support.text: Broken side passes; double solid, neither.

prompt.text: The solid yellow line is on Zoe's side and a broken yellow line is beside it. May she pass?

answer.text: No. Only the broken side may pass.

rationale.text: Broken-plus-solid yellow lets the broken side pass, while double solid yellow lets neither side pass.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on road markings and yellow lines. Road markings guide, warn and regulate traffic, and they come in red, yellow or white, used alone or combined. In this lesson we start with the colors and then focus on yellow lines, which mark two-way traffic and tell you when passing is allowed. We will compare a broken yellow center line, a broken yellow line beside a solid one, and double solid yellow lines, and we will cover the one exception that lets a driver cross from the solid side. We finish with passing on a two-lane road that has no markings at all. The pattern of the yellow line is the key to every passing question.

lines.text: Some towns: red curbs for no parking.
Red reflectors face wrong-way traffic only.

narration.text: Red markings are rare. Some towns use red curbs to mark no parking, and red pavement reflectors face wrong-way traffic only. That last detail matters: if you see red reflectors facing you, they are facing wrong-way traffic, which means you are the one heading the wrong way. Yellow and white carry the other markings in this section. Yellow marks the center of two-way roads, and white marks lanes moving the same way, along with many other markings we will see in the next lesson. Keep the colors straight first, because the color of a line tells you which kind of traffic is on its other side before you look at the pattern.

lines.text: Broken yellow: pass on the left either way when clear.
Double solid yellow: no passing either way.

narration.text: Yellow center lines mean two-way traffic moving in opposite directions. A broken yellow center line allows passing on the left in either direction when the way ahead is clear. Double solid yellow lines mark the road center between opposing flows: no passing either way. You may cross double solid yellow only for left turns, or for pedestrians, bicyclists, or scooter and skateboard riders when the opposite lane is clear and safe. So the broken yellow center opens passing to both directions, and the double solid yellow closes it to both. Between those two lies the mixed pattern, a broken line beside a solid one, which we look at next.

title.text: The solid side does not pass

lines.text: Broken beside solid: only the broken side passes.
Solid side may cross only for walkers and riders.

narration.text: Here is the trap. When a broken yellow line runs beside a solid yellow line, passing is allowed only from the broken side. Drivers on the solid side may cross only for pedestrians, bicyclists, or scooter and skateboard riders, when the opposite lane is clear and safe. So broken-plus-solid yellow lets the broken side pass, while double solid yellow lets neither side pass. Check which line is nearer to you. If the solid line is on your side, you do not cross it to pass a car. If the broken line is on your side, you may pass when clear. The exception for walkers and riders is the only reason a solid-side driver may cross.

Here is a quick check: Zoe is driving on a road where the solid yellow line is on her side and a broken yellow line runs beside it. May she cross to pass the slow car ahead? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no. A broken yellow line beside a solid yellow line allows passing only from the broken side, and Zoe is on the solid side. She may cross from the solid side only for pedestrians, bicyclists, or scooter and skateboard riders when the opposite lane is clear. If the lines were double solid yellow, neither side could pass. Broken side passes; double solid, neither.

lines.text: Unmarked two-lane road: pass on the left.

narration.text: To close the lesson, one more case: a road with no markings at all. On an unmarked two-lane road, you may pass a slow vehicle on the left where no signs prohibit passing and the way is clear. To recap: road markings guide, warn and regulate in red, yellow or white. Red is rare, and red reflectors face wrong-way traffic. Yellow center lines mean two-way traffic. A broken yellow center allows passing either way when clear. With broken beside solid, only the broken side passes. Double solid yellow means no passing either way, with crossing only for left turns or for walkers and riders. Broken side passes; double solid, neither.

why_how.text: White lines divide lanes moving the same direction and mark many positions on the road.
Arrows in your lane tell you whether you must turn or may choose, and wrong-way arrows warn of danger.

scenario.text: Ben's lane shows a curved arrow with the word ONLY.

reasoning.text: A curved arrow alone or with ONLY means you must turn that way.

result.text: Ben turns in the arrow's direction rather than going straight.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a curved arrow with ONLY still allows going straight.

correction.text: A curved arrow alone or with ONLY forces the turn, while a curved plus straight arrow offers turn or straight.

memory_support.text: ONLY means must; plus straight means may.

prompt.text: Ben's lane has a curved arrow with ONLY. May he go straight?

answer.text: No. A curved arrow with ONLY means he must turn that way.

rationale.text: A curved arrow alone or with ONLY forces the turn; only a curved plus straight arrow lets you choose.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on white lines and pavement arrows. White lines divide lanes of traffic moving in the same direction, and white is also used for stop lines, crosswalks and parking spaces. In this lesson we work through the four white line patterns: broken, dotted, solid, and double solid. Then we look at the yield line of triangles, the turn arrows that tell you what your lane may do, and the wrong-way arrows that warn you that you are driving against traffic. As with yellow lines, the pattern of a white line tells you how freely you may cross it, from careful lane changes all the way to never crossing at all.

lines.text: Broken white: same-direction lanes, change with caution.
Dotted white: lanes through intersections and interchanges.
Also turn openings, entrance and exit lanes.

narration.text: Broken white lines divide same-direction lanes, and you may change lanes across them with caution. Compare broken yellow: broken yellow divides opposing directions with passing allowed, while broken white divides same-direction lanes with changes allowed. Dotted white lines do a guiding job. They assign lanes through intersections and interchanges, guide paired turning lanes, and mark turn-lane openings and entrance and exit lanes. So broken white opens free lane changes, while dotted white steers lanes through intersections and ramps. If you see dotted lines through an intersection, follow them to stay in your assigned lane until you are through it.

lines.text: Solid white: turn lanes and right edge.
Discourages changes near intersections and ramps.
Yield triangles: where to yield or stop.

narration.text: Solid white lines mark turn lanes and the right edge of the pavement. They discourage lane changes near intersections and ramps, and they pair with arrows that dictate the allowed turn. Stop lines, crosswalks and parking spaces also use white. A yield line is a row of triangles across the road, often with a yield sign or at a roundabout entrance, and it marks where to yield or stop. So yield triangles mark a yield-or-stop point, while white stop lines, crosswalks and parking marks fix exact positions. When a solid white line separates your lane near an intersection, the arrows in your lane decide where you go next.

lines.text: Curved arrow alone or with ONLY: must turn.
Curved plus straight arrow: turn or straight.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A curved arrow in your lane, alone or with the word ONLY, means you must turn that way. A curved plus straight arrow means you may turn or go straight. The difference is between must and may. A curved arrow alone or with ONLY forces the turn, while a curved plus straight arrow offers a choice of turning or going straight. If you are in a lane marked with a curved arrow and the word ONLY, and you want to go straight, you are in the wrong lane, and the rule still requires the turn. Read the arrows early, before the solid white lines near the intersection discourage a lane change.

lines.text: Wrong-way arrows: slow down, pull over at once.
Enter only where signs and markings allow.

narration.text: Wrong-way arrows mean you are driving against traffic, toward a head-on crash. Slow down and pull over at once. Double solid white lines divide same-direction lanes, often shielding special-use lanes like HOV lanes. Never cross them; enter only where signs and markings allow. So the white line ladder runs from broken white, where you change lanes with caution, through solid white, which discourages changes near intersections and ramps, to double solid white, which you never cross. Remember the red reflectors from the last lesson as well, because they face wrong-way traffic only, just as these arrows point at drivers going the wrong way.

Here is a quick check: Ben is in a lane marked with a curved arrow and the word ONLY. He would like to go straight. May he? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no. A curved arrow alone or with ONLY means you must turn that way. Only a curved plus straight arrow lets you choose between turning and going straight. Ben must make the turn shown by the arrow. If you answered yes, you were reading the arrow as a suggestion rather than a requirement. Remember the memory line: ONLY means must, and plus straight means may. Reading the arrows early helps you choose the right lane before you reach the intersection.

lines.text: Broken: change with caution. Dotted: guidance.
Solid: discourages changes. Double solid: never cross.

narration.text: To close the lesson: broken white lines divide same-direction lanes, and you may change lanes with caution. Dotted white lines guide lanes through intersections and interchanges and mark turn, entrance and exit lanes. Solid white lines mark turn lanes and the right edge and discourage changes near intersections and ramps. Double solid white lines must never be crossed, and you enter special-use lanes only where signs and markings allow. A row of triangles marks where to yield or stop. A curved arrow alone or with ONLY means you must turn, and a curved plus straight arrow means you may choose. Wrong-way arrows mean slow down and pull over at once.

why_how.text: Three-lane roads use the center lane for left turns or passing, and its markings say which.
Some lanes are shared with bicycles or reserved for bikes, buses or high-occupancy vehicles.

scenario.text: Raj wants to turn left from a center lane marked with solid plus broken yellow lines on both sides.

reasoning.text: That center lane is open to left turns from either direction, but never to more than one hundred fifty feet of travel.

result.text: Raj enters the center lane close to his turn and travels no more than one hundred fifty feet in it.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking you may drive in a solid-plus-broken center lane for as long as you like before turning.

correction.text: A center lane with solid plus broken yellow on both sides is open to left turns from either direction, but never to more than one hundred fifty feet of travel.

memory_support.text: Broken both sides passes; solid-plus-broken turns.

prompt.text: How far may Raj travel in a solid-plus-broken center lane before turning left?

answer.text: No more than one hundred fifty feet.

rationale.text: That center lane is open to left turns from either direction, but never to more than one hundred fifty feet of travel.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on center lanes and reserved lanes. Some lanes have special jobs. On three-lane two-way roads, the marked center lane serves left turns or passing, and the yellow lines on each side tell you which. Other lanes are shared with bicycles, set aside for bicycles, or reserved for buses and high-occupancy vehicles. In this lesson we cover the two center lane patterns, sharrows, bicycle lanes and bicycle boxes, bus-only lanes, and HOV lanes with their diamond markings. Each lane has its own markings and its own rules for when an ordinary driver may enter, so the skill here is reading the marking and knowing what it allows.

lines.text: Broken yellow both sides: passing either direction.
Solid plus broken both sides: left turns either direction.
Never more than one hundred fifty feet of travel.

narration.text: On three-lane two-way roads, the marked center lane serves left turns or passing. A center lane with a broken yellow line on both sides is open to passing from either direction. A center lane with solid plus broken yellow on both sides is open to left turns from either direction, but never to more than one hundred fifty feet of travel. So a center lane broken on both sides allows passing from either way, while a center lane solid-plus-broken allows only left turns within one hundred fifty feet. The markings on the center lane's edges are the clue. Broken on both edges is a passing lane, and solid plus broken is a turn lane with a distance limit.

lines.text: Solid-plus-broken center lane: left turns only.
Travel no more than one hundred fifty feet.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A driver enters a solid-plus-broken center lane far ahead of the turn and drives along in it. The rule does not allow that. A center lane with solid plus broken yellow on both sides is open to left turns from either direction, but never to more than one hundred fifty feet of travel. It is a turn lane, not a travel lane. Compare the center lane broken on both sides, which is open to passing from either direction. If an exam question asks how far you may travel in the turn lane, the answer is no more than one hundred fifty feet. Enter it near your turn, and turn left from it.

lines.text: Sharrow: bikes ride in the narrow lane; expect them.
Bike lane: drivers enter only to turn.
Bicycle box: stop behind it on red.

narration.text: A sharrow pairs a bicycle symbol with a double chevron on lanes too narrow to share side by side. Bicyclists ride there, and drivers should expect them. Bicycle lanes, marked by solid or dashed white lines or green pavement with a bike symbol, stay preferential for bikes. Drivers enter only to turn, after mirror checks and yielding to bikes in the lane. So a sharrow shares a narrow lane with bikes riding in it, while a bike lane reserves its space with entry only for turns. Bicycle boxes at intersections hold waiting riders ahead of drivers: stop behind the box on red, never inside it, and make no right on red there.

lines.text: Bus-only: BUS ONLY markings, red pavement, or both.
HOV: center diamonds, posted passengers and hours.
A diamond can also reserve a lane for buses.

narration.text: Bus-only lanes carry BUS ONLY markings, red-colored pavement, or both. HOV lanes carry center diamonds and may run barrier-separated or behind double white lines. In heavy traffic they serve buses, vanpools, carpools, high-occupancy vehicles, motorcycles and certain clean-fuel vehicles, with signs posting the minimum passengers and the hours, and barrier lanes reverse direction by time of day. A diamond marking can also reserve a lane for buses. So center diamonds open HOV lanes to qualified high-occupancy travel, while BUS ONLY paint and red pavement close bus lanes to all but buses. Read the signs for passengers and hours before entering an HOV lane.

lines.text: How far may you travel in it?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Raj is on a three-lane road and wants to turn left from a center lane marked with solid plus broken yellow lines on both sides. How far may he travel in that lane before turning? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no more than one hundred fifty feet. That center lane is open to left turns from either direction, but never to more than one hundred fifty feet of travel. Raj should enter it near his turn. If the lane had broken yellow on both sides instead, it would be a passing lane open to traffic from either direction. Broken both sides passes; solid-plus-broken turns.

lines.text: On green: signal right turns, yield to bikes.

narration.text: To close the lesson: at a bicycle box, stop behind the box on red and never inside it, make no right on red there, and on green signal your right turn and yield to bikes on the right. On three-lane roads, a center lane broken on both sides is for passing, and one with solid plus broken lines is for left turns with no more than one hundred fifty feet of travel. A sharrow means bikes ride in the lane, and a bike lane is entered only to turn. Bus-only lanes show BUS ONLY markings or red pavement, and HOV lanes show diamonds, with signs posting passengers and hours. Broken both sides passes; solid-plus-broken turns.

why_how.text: Message boards, rumble strips and slow moving vehicle signs each ask for a specific response.
Toll lanes and curb colors have their own rules that are easy to mix up.

scenario.text: Mia has no E-ZPass transponder and enters a high-speed E-ZPass lane by mistake.

reasoning.text: High-speed E-ZPass lanes are transponder-only, and a mistaken entry must never stop, since cameras photograph the plate and bill the registered owner.

result.text: Mia keeps going without stopping, and the registered owner is billed.

claim.text: Common mistake: stopping in a high-speed E-ZPass lane after entering it by mistake.

correction.text: A mistaken entry must never stop; cameras photograph the plate and bill the registered owner.

memory_support.text: Purple pays, cash pays, never stop at speed.

prompt.text: Mia enters a high-speed E-ZPass lane without a transponder. Should she stop?

answer.text: No. She must never stop; cameras photograph the plate and bill the owner.

rationale.text: High-speed E-ZPass lanes are transponder-only, and a mistaken entry must never stop.

narration.text: Welcome to the last lesson of this section. We cover messages on and beside the road, toll lanes, and painted curbs. Message boards report traffic, road and weather hazards. Rumble strips give you a warning through the road surface. Slow moving vehicle signs mark vehicles that travel at low speed. Then we look at Virginia toll facilities, which all accept E-ZPass, and the special rule for high-speed E-ZPass lanes. Finally, painted curbs, where white, yellow and red each set a different parking rule that you should confirm with the locality. Each of these items asks something specific of you, and the details are what the exam asks about.

lines.text: Rumble strips: slowly and straight, never swerve.
Slow moving vehicles: adjust speed or position.

narration.text: Portable and permanent message boards report traffic, road and weather hazards. Always obey their directions. Rumble strip warnings mean driving slowly and straight over the strips, never swerving around them. So message boards issue directions to obey, while rumble strips issue a surface to cross slowly and straight. Slow moving vehicles, those moving at twenty-five miles per hour or less, such as farm equipment, horse-drawn vehicles and work vehicles, display warning signs. Adjust your speed or position for them. When you come up behind a vehicle showing that sign, expect it to be moving at twenty-five miles per hour or less, and plan your speed or position early.

Every Virginia toll facility accepts E-ZPass transponders. If you have one, follow the lanes marked with the purple logo. If you do not, follow the cash lanes. As you go through the toll area, slow down and use caution for drivers changing lanes and for employees crossing. The two kinds of lanes sort drivers by payment, and the manual's instruction is simple: purple-logo lanes for transponder holders, cash lanes for everyone else. Then there is a third kind of lane, the high-speed E-ZPass lane, which is transponder-only and has a rule of its own for drivers who enter it by mistake. That rule is the subject of the next slide.

lines.text: Cameras photograph the plate, owner is billed.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A driver without a transponder realizes they have entered a high-speed E-ZPass lane and stops or backs up to fix the mistake. The rule says never stop. High-speed E-ZPass lanes are transponder-only, and a mistaken entry must never stop, since cameras photograph the plate and bill the registered owner. So purple-logo lanes serve transponder holders and cash lanes serve the rest, while high-speed transponder lanes punish a mistaken entry with no stopping. The billing is handled by the cameras and the plate, so the driver's job is to keep moving. Stopping in a high-speed lane is the one thing the rule forbids.

Here is a quick check: Mia has no E-ZPass transponder, and she enters a high-speed E-ZPass lane by mistake. Should she stop to sort it out? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no. High-speed E-ZPass lanes are transponder-only, and a mistaken entry must never stop, since cameras photograph the plate and bill the registered owner. Mia keeps moving, and the registered owner of the car is billed. Without a transponder, the lanes Mia should have followed are the cash lanes. With a transponder, she would follow the purple-logo lanes. Purple pays, cash pays, and you never stop at speed in a high-speed lane.

lines.text: White: passenger pickup and dropoff only.
Red: no stopping, standing or parking.

narration.text: To close the section, painted curbs. Painted curbs set parking rules, which you should confirm with the locality. A white curb allows only passenger pickup and dropoff. A yellow curb allows only loading, with the driver staying. A red curb bans stopping, standing and parking. So white curbs serve passenger pickup and dropoff, yellow curbs serve loading with the driver present, and red curbs ban stopping, standing and parking. To recap the lesson: obey message boards, cross rumble strips slowly and straight, adjust for slow moving vehicles, use purple-logo lanes with a transponder and cash lanes without one, and never stop in a high-speed E-ZPass lane.
